transcript.text: Clearing out a drawer I found a letter from 2020 saying my Hotpoint washing machine might be part of a fire safety recall. Model WMXTF 742P UK. It's been working fine all this time - do I really need to do anything?

Yes, I'd really encourage you to act on it. A machine working fine tells you nothing about this kind of fault. Fire safety recalls are issued because a part can fail suddenly and without warning, even on a machine that has behaved perfectly for years. The letter is a few years old, but if your machine is covered, the remedy should still be available. Recall remedies are free. From memory, the Hotpoint and Indesit washing machine recall around that time was about the door-lock mechanism overheating. Not every machine with a given model name was included, though. It usually comes down to when it was made, which is why the letter probably says 'might'. The serial number is what settles it. What to do:
1. Find the rating label. It's usually on the inside rim of the door opening (open the door and look around the frame) or on the back. Note the model number and the serial number.
2. Put them into Hotpoint's (Whirlpool's) official recall checker online, or ring the phone number on your letter. You can also search GOV.UK product safety alerts for Hotpoint washing machines.
3. If it comes back as affected, unplug it and stop using it until the manufacturer has done the remedy. Don't run it overnight or while you're out in the meantime.
4. If it comes back as not affected, carry on as normal. It's worth keeping a note of the result with the letter. Until you know either way, the safest choice is to only run it while you're home and awake. Unplug it when you're not using it. Let me know what the checker says. If it's affected, I can explain what usually happens next.

Ok, I've found the label inside the door and the serial number is readable. I haven't used the recall checker yet, so I'm not sure where to find it. I do often run it overnight or while I'm out, as it's in the kitchen. Until I know, is it ok to still do cold washes if I'm home?

Honestly, a cold wash doesn't make it much safer. The concern with that recall was the door-lock mechanism overheating, not the heater, and the door lock works on every wash whatever the temperature. So I wouldn't treat cold washes as a safe workaround. Checking only takes a few minutes, and that's far better than guessing. 1. Search online for "Hotpoint washing machine recall" and use the result on Hotpoint's own UK website (hotpoint.co.uk). Avoid look-alike sites. Enter the model number and the serial number from the label inside the door. It tells you straight away whether your machine is affected.
2. Have the model and serial number ready.
3. GOV.UK's product safety alerts page also lists the recall, if you want to confirm it independently. Search there for Hotpoint washing machine. - Affected: unplug the machine at the wall and stop using it. Hotpoint will arrange the free remedy.
• Not affected: carry on as normal, overnight runs included. - Only run it while you're in and awake, ideally nearby.
• Don't leave it running overnight or while you're out. I'd pause that habit until you have an answer.
• Unplug it at the wall when it finishes.
• Make sure your smoke alarm is working. Let me know what the checker says. If it comes back as affected, I'll explain what usually happens next.

Ok, thank you, that makes sense. I'll stop running it overnight and when I'm out, and I'll go and look up the checker now. Is there anything else I should have ready besides the model and serial number?

The model and serial number are the main things, and the checker normally needs only those. A few extras make it smoother if the machine turns out to be affected: 1. A photo of the rating label. It's easy to misread a digit, and a clear photo lets you re-enter it or read it out over the phone.
2. The 2020 letter. If it has a reference number or a dedicated helpline number, keep it to hand. That can link your record and speed things up.
3. Your contact details: name, address with postcode, phone number and email. If you're affected, they'll use these to book the free remedy, which is usually a home visit.
4. A rough idea of when it's convenient for someone to come, and how easy the machine is to get at. For example, whether it's built in under a worktop. You don't normally need a receipt or proof of purchase for a safety recall. It's tied to the machine itself, not who bought it or when. What the result means: - If it says affected, unplug the machine at the wall and stop using it until the remedy is done. The checker or helpline should explain the next steps.
• If it says not affected, you can go back to using it normally. If the website won't accept the serial number, ring the number on the letter instead. They can check it for you. Let me know what it comes back with.
